Home.title: SAFETYHOKAIDO
Home.subtitle: Hokkaido Disaster Guide for Tourist
Home.aboutText: In addition to real-time updates on weather and disaster alerts—which are useful for your trip to Hokkaido—we also provide easy-to-understand travel guides.
Home.pleaseSelect: Please select what you'd like to know.
Home.infoText: Hokkaido is the northernmost island of Japan. It is famous for beautiful nature and cold, snowy winters. The largest city is Sapporo, known for its snow festival. Hokkaido also has delicious food, such as fresh seafood and dairy products.

Car.title: RENTAL CAR
Car.step1Desc: You cannot drive in Japan with only your home country's license. You need an International Driving Permit (IDP) based on the 1949 Geneva Convention, or an official Japanese translation for some countries.
Car.step2Desc: At the rental counter, show your IDP, home license, and passport. Staff will check the car with you and explain the return rules.
Car.step3Desc: In Japan, drive on the left side of the road. Come to a full stop at every stop sign (a red triangle). Everyone must wear a seatbelt, and using a phone while driving is banned.
Car.step4Desc: Fill up before returning the car, and keep the receipt — most rentals require a full tank on return. Park only in marked parking lots or metered spaces.
Car.step5Desc: Return the car to the agreed place by the agreed time, with a full tank. Staff will check the car and fuel. If you'll be late, call the rental company as early as possible.
Car.linkDesc: Public Transportation Service Updates in Hokkaido

Bus.title: BUS
Bus.step1Desc: Find the bus stop and check the route number and destination shown on the front of the bus.
Bus.step2Desc: In Hokkaido, you usually get on from the rear (back) door. As you board, take a small "seiriken" (numbered ticket) from the machine by the door.
Bus.step3Desc: A screen at the front shows fares under each ticket number. As the bus travels, the fare next to your seiriken number goes up. Watch this screen so you know how much to pay when you get off.
Bus.step4Desc: When you hear or see your stop, press one of the "stop" buttons on the wall or handrail. This tells the driver to stop.
Bus.step5Desc: Get off from the front door and pay as you leave.
Bus.link2Desc: Check bus routes and times on the official JR Hokkaido Bus site.

Train.title: TRAIN
Train.step1Desc: At the station, buy a ticket from the ticket machine, or use an IC card such as Kitaca or Suica.
Train.step2Desc: Go through the ticket gate to enter. With a paper ticket, insert it into the slot and take it back on the other side.
Train.step3Desc: Line up on the platform and let people off first. Keep your ticket safe until you exit.
Train.step4Desc: At your destination, go through the ticket gate again.
Train.link2Desc: Check train times and delays on the official JR Hokkaido site.

LearningMaterials.title:
LEARNING
MATERIALS
LearningMaterials.alertsTitle: What are weather and disaster alerts?
LearningMaterials.alertsDesc: In Japan, the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issues official alerts when dangerous weather or a disaster is expected. They tell you how serious the situation is, so you can decide what to do. Alerts come in levels, and the stronger the word, the more dangerous the situation.
LearningMaterials.mainLevelsDesc: Alerts generally rise through three stages.
LearningMaterials.level1Desc:
Conditions could cause minor problems.
→ Stay aware and check updates.
LearningMaterials.level2Desc:
Dangerous conditions are expected.
→ Avoid unnecessary travel.
LearningMaterials.level3Desc:
Used for rare, extreme events.
→ Act now to protect yourself.
LearningMaterials.powerIntro: Earthquakes and heavy snow can both cut the power, sometimes across a wide area. In 2018, a large earthquake left almost all of Hokkaido without electricity. In winter, a power outage is especially serious because it also stops the heating — staying warm becomes a safety issue, not just a comfort one.
LearningMaterials.prep1: Keep your phone charged and carry a power bank.
LearningMaterials.prep2: Have some cash — cards and ATMs may not work.
LearningMaterials.prep3: Keep a flashlight or light source handy.
LearningMaterials.out1: Check official information (JMA, NHK WORLD, the Safety tips app) for updates.
LearningMaterials.out2: Save your phone battery, but keep it on for alerts.
LearningMaterials.out3: If your room becomes unsafe, move to a designated shelter or a large public facility.
LearningMaterials.helpDeskIntro: Useful resources for tourists during emergencies or for travel planning in Hokkaido.

Blizzard.title: DISASTER
Blizzard.whatIsItDesc: A blizzard is a severe snowstorm with strong winds. The wind blows snow through the air, making it difficult to see and travel safely.
Blizzard.hotelRoomDesc: Do not go outside while a heavy snow or blizzard warning is in effect. Change or delay your plans. Check the weather forecast and transport status before you leave.
Blizzard.wantToGoOut: If you still want to go out in heavy snow
Blizzard.wantToGoOutDesc: Wear warm layers, and cover your skin with a hat, gloves, and scarf. Stay close by and avoid going far.
Blizzard.outsideDesc: Check train and bus status before you head back — delays and cancellations are common in heavy snow. The subway is the most reliable option, as it runs underground and is less affected by snow.
Blizzard.cantGetBackDesc: Don't force your way through a blizzard. Find a warm place to stay and wait it out. If you can't return to your hotel, contact them, and look for a nearby hotel if needed.
Blizzard.link1Desc: Find the nearest evacuation shelter from your location.
Blizzard.link2Desc: Official weather warnings, including heavy snow, in multiple languages.
Blizzard.blzCanHappenIntro: During heavy snow in Hokkaido, you may experience:
Blizzard.blzCanHappen1: Trains, buses, and flights delayed or cancelled — sometimes for a full day.
Blizzard.blzCanHappen2: Roads and highways closed, with taxis and rental cars unable to run.
Blizzard.blzCanHappen3: Whiteout conditions where you can't see, even on city streets.
Blizzard.blzNowOutside1: Get indoors now — any shop, station, or building. Don't push on to your destination.
Blizzard.blzNowOutside2: In a whiteout, don't keep walking. You can get lost within meters, even in a city.
Blizzard.blzNowCar: If you're caught in a car
Blizzard.blzNowCar1: Stay with the car. Don't walk off to find help.
Blizzard.blzNowCar2: Keep the exhaust pipe clear of snow, or deadly gas can enter the car.
Blizzard.blzNowCar3: Call for help: 110, or your rental company. Turn on hazard lights.

Earthquake.title: EARTHQUAKE
Earthquake.whatIsItDesc: Japan is one of the most earthquake-prone countries in the world, so shaking can happen at any time. It can make it hard to stand or move safely.
Earthquake.tsunamiBanner:
Near the coast?
There's more you need to know.
Earthquake.tsunamiWhatIsItDesc: A tsunami is a series of powerful waves caused by an earthquake under the sea. It can arrive within minutes, so if you feel strong shaking near the coast, move to high ground right away.
Earthquake.link1Desc: Find the nearest evacuation shelter from your location.
Earthquake.eqCanHappenIntro: During or after an earthquake in Hokkaido, you may experience:
Earthquake.eqCanHappen1: Trains and subways stopping, and airport delays or closures.
Earthquake.eqCanHappen2: Water outages and mobile networks becoming hard to use.
Earthquake.eqCanHappen3: Falling objects, broken glass, and furniture tipping over indoors.
Earthquake.eqNowWhile1: Drop, cover, and hold on. Get under a sturdy table and protect your head and neck.
Earthquake.eqNowWhile3: Outdoors: move away from buildings, walls, and power lines, and cover your head.
Earthquake.eqNowWhen1: Check yourself and people nearby for injuries.
Earthquake.eqNowWhen2: Put on shoes — there may be broken glass.
Earthquake.eqNowWhen3: Open a door to keep an exit, and expect aftershocks.
Earthquake.tsNow1: If you are near the coast and feel strong shaking, or long slow shaking, go to high ground immediately.
Earthquake.tsNow2: Don't wait for a warning, and don't go to check the sea.
Earthquake.tsNow3: Go as high and as far inland as you can, on foot — roads may be blocked.
Earthquake.tsNow4: Stay high. Waves come again and again, and the first is often not the largest.
Earthquake.tsCanHappenIntro: If an earthquake triggers a tsunami near the coast, you may experience:
Earthquake.tsCanHappen1: Powerful waves that reach the shore within minutes of the shaking.
Earthquake.tsCanHappen2: Water that rushes far inland, well beyond normal beaches and rivers.
Earthquake.tsCanHappen3: Strong currents that make it impossible to stand or swim.
